strengths: The method addresses a relevant problem: using temporal information in critic learning while retaining a reactive, step-based policy. Predicting returns for multiple action prefixes is a plausible auxiliary learning approach.

The reported results are promising: Table 1 gives 86% Meta-World success versus 70% for SAC and PPO, and 92% dense box-pushing success versus 60% for the strongest listed baseline. Per-task learning curves provide useful detail.
The paper includes policy-component ablations, an MLP-critic comparison, and substantial hyperparameter tables, providing some evidence beyond aggregate benchmark scores.
weaknesses: The central variance-reduction justification is unsupported. Equation (4) concerns averaging scalar return targets, whereas Equation (7) averages gradients from different outputs with different parameter Jacobians. The former does not establish reduced variance for the latter or preservation of sparse reward signals. Correlations among bootstrapped values and between rewards and values are also omitted. Moreover, O(N/3) remains O(N), so the analysis provides no improved asymptotic scaling.

Novelty relative to TOP-ERL is limited and insufficiently isolated. The paper explicitly adopts its Transformer critic and action-sequence return prediction, principally replacing the episodic policy with a reactive SAC policy. There is no direct TOP-ERL comparison or sufficiently detailed analysis establishing what new mechanism accounts for the gains.

The ablations do not separate the main proposed ingredients. Missing comparisons include a one-step Transformer critic, conventional multi-step SAC, an MLP or recurrent critic conditioned on action chunks, and a sequence-length sweep. The SAC-variant experiment is useful but does not clearly specify whether it retains equivalent multi-horizon supervision, and it changes architecture and temporal conditioning together.

The algorithm is incompletely specified. The bootstrapped value V is not explicitly defined in terms of the critic, policy, entropy, and twin-critic minimum; terminal masking is absent from the equations; and Equation (6) uses G^(n) for prefixes that should have different horizons. The claimed elimination of importance sampling also needs assumptions: conditioning on replayed action sequences does not generally establish unbiased open-loop sequence values in stochastic environments with feedback behavior policies.

Evaluation uncertainty and generalization protocols are inadequately documented. Table 1 lacks confidence intervals; seed counts are not consistently reported beyond a specific ablation; plot shading and evaluation episode counts are unspecified; and the Meta-World ML1 training/test goal protocol is unclear. Success across separately trained tasks alone does not substantiate the claimed generalization.

Several headline claims exceed the evidence. Sparse box-pushing success is 58%, below gSDE's 60%, contradicting claims of state-of-the-art performance there. The per-task curves also show substantial weaknesses on tasks such as ButtonPress, Reach, and PickPlaceWall, contrary to claims of strong performance across all tasks. No direct measurements establish more accurate value estimates or smoother value surfaces.

Efficiency and comparison fairness remain uncertain. Methods differ substantially in update schedules, optimizers, network sizes, and discount factors, without a documented tuning budget or runtime comparison. T-SAC also disables entropy regularization in both box-pushing settings. These choices complicate attribution of improvements to the proposed SAC critic, and the missing sparse-task chunk-length settings further limit reproducibility.

strengths: The approach is practically motivated: training a causal Transformer critic on action prefixes and multiple return horizons while retaining a reactive SAC policy could improve temporal credit assignment without requiring an episodic actor.

The reported empirical gains are substantial on some benchmarks: Table 1 shows 86% aggregate Meta-World success versus 70% for SAC, and 92% dense box-pushing success versus 60% for the strongest listed baseline.

The evaluation covers 50 Meta-World tasks, provides per-task learning curves and hyperparameter tables, and includes useful ablations of policy normalization, covariance conditioning, entropy regularization, and an MLP-critic variant.
weaknesses: The central variance-reduction justification does not establish the claimed property of the proposed algorithm. Section 2.3 analyzes averaged scalar returns under approximately independent rewards, whereas training averages gradients of different predictions with different inputs and Jacobians. Their variance depends on gradient covariances, which are neither analyzed nor measured. The bootstrap variance term also omits potentially substantial correlations between value estimates and rewards. Averaging loss gradients does not by itself guarantee preservation of sparse reward signals.

The novelty over TOP-ERL is insufficiently established. The paper explicitly adopts its Transformer critic and multi-step trajectory supervision, with the main distinction being a reactive SAC actor. There is no direct TOP-ERL comparison, and the experiments do not isolate Transformer architecture from multi-horizon supervision through one-step Transformer, multi-step MLP/recurrent, or sequence-length ablations.

The theoretical meaning of the sequence-conditioned critic is underdeveloped. Conditioning on recorded action sequences changes the value function being learned; the paper does not specify conditions under which replay trajectories provide valid targets without importance correction, particularly with stochastic transitions and feedback-generated actions. Since policy optimization uses only Q(s,a), the claimed benefits of longer-prefix predictions depend on shared representations, but that transfer is not directly demonstrated.

Several headline claims exceed the evidence. Sparse box-pushing success is 58%, below gSDE's 60%, so Table 1 does not establish superiority there. The per-task curves also contradict consistently strong performance across all tasks, with weak results on tasks such as PickPlaceWall and ButtonPress. Generalization claims lack a clearly described held-out evaluation protocol, and smoother or more accurate value estimates are not measured.

Experimental uncertainty and comparison fairness are inadequately documented. Table 1 provides no uncertainty estimates; the seed counts, evaluation episode counts, and meaning of shaded intervals are not consistently specified. Architectures, optimization schedules, and other hyperparameters differ substantially, without a documented tuning budget or wall-clock comparison. The SAC-variant ablation helps, but does not resolve these concerns or establish computational efficiency.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous despite the hyperparameter tables. Equation (6) labels every prefix target G^(n), although the prose requires G^(i+1); the bootstrapped soft value and terminal masking are not explicitly defined. The relationship between the stated UTD ratio, update schedules, and tabulated epochs is unclear. Box-pushing experiments disable entropy regularization, an important departure from the advertised SAC formulation.

strengths: The approach is well motivated: training a causal Transformer critic on action prefixes and multiple return horizons could improve temporal credit assignment while retaining a reactive SAC policy.

The reported empirical gains are substantial on MetaWorld (86% aggregate success versus 70% for SAC) and dense box pushing (92% versus 60% for the strongest reported baseline). Per-task learning curves provide useful additional evidence.
The paper includes policy-component ablations, an MLP-critic replacement experiment, and extensive hyperparameter tables. These are useful steps toward understanding and reproducing the results.
weaknesses: The central variance-reduction argument does not establish the claimed property of the algorithm. Equation (4) concerns averaged return targets, whereas Equation (7) averages gradients of different predictions with different inputs and Jacobians. The former does not imply the latter has reduced variance or avoids sparse-reward dilution. Correlations between bootstrap estimates and rewards are also omitted, and O(N/3) is still O(N). Neither a suitable gradient-variance analysis nor direct measurements substantiate this central claim.

Novelty relative to TOP-ERL is insufficiently established. The paper explicitly adopts its Transformer critic and multi-step sequence-learning approach; the main distinction is integration with a reactive SAC policy. A direct comparison or controlled adaptation of TOP-ERL is missing, leaving the significance of this extension unclear.

The ablations do not adequately isolate the proposed mechanism. Replacing the Transformer with an MLP is useful, but the sequence inputs and multi-horizon supervision retained in that replacement are underspecified. Missing controls include a one-step Transformer critic, an MLP with comparable multi-step supervision, and a sequence-length sweep. Consequently, the gains cannot confidently be attributed to critic chunking or the proposed gradient-averaging explanation.

Several performance claims exceed the evidence. Table 1 reports 58% sparse box-pushing success for T-SAC versus 60% for gSDE, contradicting the claimed new benchmark on that setting. Appendix curves also show substantial task-dependent weaknesses, including ButtonPress and Reach, rather than consistently superior performance. Generalization claims lack a clearly specified held-out evaluation protocol.

Statistical reporting is inadequate for assessing reliability. Table 1 provides no uncertainty estimates; seed counts and evaluation episode counts are not systematically documented, and the shaded learning-curve intervals are not clearly defined. The description of IQM as requiring 75% convergence is also misleading. These omissions particularly undermine claims of improved stability and small performance differences.

Important implementation and comparison details remain ambiguous. Equation (6) labels every prefix target G^(n), although the surrounding text calls for horizon-specific targets; the bootstrap value computation and terminal handling are not fully specified. The update schedule in Section 4.3.4 is difficult to reconcile with the hyperparameter tables, and box-pushing experiments disable T-SAC's entropy term despite the general automatic-tuning description. Runtime, compute-matched comparisons, and a documented tuning budget are absent. Overall, the promising results do not yet overcome the unresolved methodological and evaluation weaknesses required for acceptance.

strengths: The method addresses a useful problem: exploiting multi-step supervision while retaining a reactive, one-step actor. A shared causal Transformer that predicts action-prefix values is a plausible and practical design.

The reported manipulation results are promising, particularly on challenging Meta-World tasks and dense Box-Pushing, where T-SAC reaches 96.8% success. Evaluation spans 57 tasks and includes multiple seeds, confidence intervals, per-task curves, and training-time measurements.

The paper provides substantial architectural and hyperparameter details, plus ablations covering sequence length, masking, recurrent alternatives, and policy-side chunking. It also acknowledges weaker locomotion performance and instability under sparse rewards.
weaknesses: The claimed target-network-free contribution is misleading. Section 4.4 explicitly snapshots the critic and freezes its bootstrap predictions for K updates. This retains the essential mechanism of a periodically refreshed target network, even if predictions are cached instead of keeping a separate network resident. It does not establish a distinct target-free stabilization method comparable to CrossQ.

The variance analysis does not establish the claimed mechanism. Gradient-level averaging is ordinary differentiation of a mean loss; Appendix D assumes equal gradient variances and equicorrelation without validating these assumptions. Gradients of different horizon objectives need not estimate the same quantity. Its claimed compounded benefit additionally invokes target averaging, which the implementation explicitly does not perform. Appendix C also contains mathematical errors: Proposition 1's limit is 3, not 4, when reward correlation is zero and gamma is 1, and the stated condition for total variance reduction omits the relative magnitudes of reward and bootstrap variances.

The assertion that conditioning on recorded action prefixes eliminates the need for importance sampling requires qualification. In stochastic environments, later actions selected by a feedback behavior policy reveal information about intermediate transitions; conditioning on these actions can therefore produce behavior-dependent conditional returns rather than policy-independent open-loop action-sequence values. Deterministic dynamics can avoid this issue, but that restriction is not stated or tested. The one-step output still receives a one-step target, so benefits to the actor arise through shared representation learning rather than a demonstrated unbiased multi-step update to its value estimate.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. T-SAC also changes entropy treatment, actor normalization, initialization, optimizer, update scheduling, and replay sampling. Most ablations concern one dense Box-Pushing task. Missing controls include an otherwise matched one-step learner and a causally valid MLP prefix critic with the same multi-horizon supervision and one-step actor. The MLP action-chunking comparison changes the policy too; conditioning a chunk-value function on its complete proposed chunk is not inherently causal leakage.

The strongest aggregate evidence has unresolved comparability issues. Appendix J imports many Meta-World baseline results from prior publications or released runs under merely 'comparable' settings, while the manuscript uses terminal-only success and a particular taskwise IQM aggregation. It does not establish that all imported results were evaluated and reaggregated identically. T-SAC receives extensive tuning without comparable Meta-World baseline searches. Broad claims of consistent superiority also exceed the results: performance is weaker on several locomotion tasks and below TOP-ERL on sparse Box-Pushing.

The theoretical explanation and implementation description are inconsistent. Equation 7 predicts multiple endpoints from one starting state, whereas Appendix G analyzes multiple starting states sharing one endpoint and bootstrap value. Its target-reuse and sparse-reward propagation arguments therefore do not directly analyze the proposed objective. Algorithm 1 also stops stored segments at termination, while Figure 12 describes concatenating episodes and masking boundaries. These discrepancies matter for reproducing the method.

Novelty remains insufficiently distinguished from TOP-ERL's existing Transformer prefix critic and multi-step supervision. The step-based actor adaptation is useful, but ordinary loss averaging and periodic target refreshes do not independently establish substantial methodological novelty. Code is promised only upon acceptance, leaving the consequential implementation ambiguities unresolved during review.

strengths: The practical idea is useful: train a causal Transformer critic on multiple action-prefix horizons while retaining a conventional one-step actor. This offers temporal supervision without requiring open-loop action execution.

The reported manipulation results are promising, particularly the Meta-World aggregate and difficult multiphase tasks, and 96.8% success on dense Box-Pushing. Evaluation spans 57 tasks and includes multiple seeds, confidence intervals, and per-task curves.

The paper provides substantial architectural and training ablations, comparisons with recurrent critics, runtime measurements, pseudocode, and hyperparameter tables. It also acknowledges weaker locomotion and sparse-reward results.
weaknesses: The general justification for eliminating importance sampling is incomplete (§4.1.2). In a stochastic environment, subsequent actions from a feedback behavior policy reveal information about intervening states. Conditioning on the realized action prefix therefore need not produce the same trajectory distribution as executing that prefix open-loop, and the learned conditional return can remain behavior-dependent. Deterministic dynamics can avoid this issue, but the paper neither states the necessary restriction nor establishes general consistency. Causal attention alone does not resolve this distinction.

The 'target-free' contribution is overstated (§4.4). The method snapshots the critic, caches bootstrap values, and holds them fixed for several optimization steps. This retains the essential mechanism of a periodically refreshed target network, even if the snapshot is discarded after caching. Removing continuous Polyak updates is a defensible claim; equating this with CrossQ-style target-network removal is not.

The variance analysis does not establish the claimed mechanism. Gradient-level averaging in Eq. (4) is simply differentiation of a mean loss. Appendix D assumes equal gradient variances and equicorrelation without empirical verification; its basic covariance identity is not Transformer-specific. Theorem 5 additionally claims compounded benefits from target averaging, although the implemented algorithm explicitly does not average targets. Its assertion that the reward-side variance ratio approaches four also contradicts Appendix C's fixed-discount limit of one.

Novelty over TOP-ERL and action-prefix value learning is insufficiently isolated. The critic architecture and prefix supervision closely follow acknowledged prior work, while averaging horizon losses is standard optimization. Adapting these components to a one-step actor may be valuable, but the paper needs stronger evidence identifying what this adaptation contributes beyond the existing ingredients.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the source of improvement. Missing controls include a capacity-matched, prefix-conditioned MLP with valid masking and a carefully matched multi-step SAC variant. Removing self-attention while invalidating the conditioning objective is not an informative architecture comparison. Moreover, evaluating an intended action chunk with an MLP is not inherently 'causal leakage,' contrary to §5.5.3. Actor normalization, optimizer, entropy handling, and capacity also change; Box-Pushing uses a four-layer, 512-unit T-SAC actor versus smaller SAC actors.

Benchmark comparability requires stronger documentation. Appendix J imports many Meta-World baselines from prior publications or released runs under merely 'comparable' settings, while this paper uses terminal-only success and a particular task-wise IQM aggregation. Exact protocol alignment and raw-result reaggregation are not established. Extensive T-SAC tuning, unequal baseline tuning, and truncating CrossQ's Box-Pushing budget further limit conclusions about superiority.

Several explanations and reproducibility details are inconsistent. Appendix G analyzes multiple starting states sharing one endpoint, whereas the main objective uses one starting state and multiple endpoints. Tables 2–3 set T-SAC's entropy coefficient to zero despite the general automatic-temperature description. Code is deferred until acceptance. Finally, the abstract's consistent-outperformance claim exceeds the evidence: locomotion results are mixed, and sparse Box-Pushing trails TOP-ERL, 58% versus 70%.

strengths: The method offers a useful practical direction: train a sequence-conditioned critic with multiple prediction horizons while retaining a reactive, one-step policy.
The reported manipulation results are promising, including strong Meta-World aggregate performance and 96.8% success on dense Box-Pushing. Evaluating 57 tasks provides substantial empirical breadth.
The experiments include multiple seeds, confidence intervals, runtime measurements, and ablations of attention, masking, prediction horizons, recurrent backbones, and policy-side chunking.
The paper acknowledges weaker locomotion results and instability under sparse rewards, and supplies extensive architecture and hyperparameter details.
weaknesses: The variance-reduction justification has substantive problems. Gradient-level averaging is simply differentiation of the mean loss; its variance benefit assumes equal variances and exchangeable correlations that are not empirically established. Appendix D additionally claims compounded benefits from target averaging, although the implementation explicitly does not average targets. There are concrete mathematical errors: Proposition 1's limit of 4 excludes the uncorrelated case, whose limit is 3, and Appendix D incorrectly repeats the limit of 4 for fixed discount factors below 1, where the ratio tends to 1.

The target-free contribution is overstated. Section 4.4 snapshots critic parameters and caches bootstrap values for subsequent updates. This retains a frozen target function and is effectively periodic hard target updating, even if a separate network need not remain in memory. It does not establish removal of the target mechanism in the sense claimed by comparison with CrossQ.

The unconditional argument that action-prefix conditioning eliminates the need for importance sampling requires qualification. In stochastic environments, later behavior-policy actions reveal information about intermediate states, so conditioning on recorded actions need not recover the value of executing that action sequence. The paper should distinguish replay-conditional auxiliary regression from policy-independent sequence-value estimation and state the assumptions supporting its interpretation.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. T-SAC also changes entropy treatment, policy normalization, optimization, initialization, and replay/update scheduling. Most ablations cover only dense Box-Pushing. A matched SAC baseline and a prefix-conditioned MLP trained with the same multi-horizon objective are needed. An action-chunk critic conditioning on its entire proposed chunk is not intrinsically suffering from causal leakage, contrary to Section 5.5.3.

Meta-World baseline comparability remains insufficiently established. Appendix J imports many results from prior publications or released runs under merely 'comparable' settings, while this paper emphasizes terminal-only success and a particular aggregation procedure. It needs explicit confirmation that all reused runs support identical evaluation and aggregation, together with clearer accounting of tuning and computation.

The explanations and algorithm are not fully consistent. Appendix G analyzes targets with different starting states and a shared endpoint, whereas Equation 7 uses a shared starting state and different endpoints. Consequently, its bootstrap-reuse and sparse-reward propagation analysis does not directly explain the implemented objective. The pseudocode, freezing schedule, and hyperparameter tables also need a clearer mapping to the claimed update-to-data ratios. Code is deferred until acceptance.

The strongest claims exceed the evidence. T-SAC trails TOP-ERL on sparse Box-Pushing, is weaker on Hopper and Walker2d, and is middling on Ant. The architectural ingredients closely follow existing Transformer critics and multi-step learning; establishing a competitive contribution therefore requires stronger causal attribution and more reliable theoretical support than currently provided.
